title: Your balance sheet is the first project you manage
summary: A developer's personal wealth is a project with its own risks: what you own, what you owe, how fast you can turn it into cash, and how much of it rides on one bet. This lesson builds the personal balance sheet from first principles and introduces the liquidity floor and concentration. It ends with a question only you can answer: what is enough?
body:
Net worth tells you how rich you look; liquidity and concentration tell you whether you survive a bad year. Manage your personal balance sheet with the same discipline you would bring to a project you were paid to run.

Recall

Q. When you answer a hostile question in a meeting, what are the three moves, in order?

A. Acknowledge the concern, bridge to what you know, then answer with the fact. If you do not have the fact, give a firm date: "I'll confirm by Friday."

Q. What does "bottom line first" mean in a spoken update?

A. State the conclusion in the first sentence, then give the two or three reasons that support it. The listener should be able to stop after one sentence and still know your answer.

Q. What is a go/no-go gate in the development lifecycle?

A. A fixed decision point where you stop, check the evidence against criteria set in advance, and either commit more money or walk away. Its value is that the criteria were written before you fell in love with the deal.

Why this matters

Developers are paid for taking concentrated, illiquid, long-dated risk. That is the job. The danger is that the same risk quietly spreads from the project into your personal life. Your salary, your equity in the deal, your personal guarantee on the loan and the value of your home can all depend on the same local market in the same year. When that market turns, they fall together. The people who last in this business are rarely the ones with the highest returns. They are the ones who were never forced to sell at the bottom. That starts with a personal balance sheet you actually read.

The balance sheet: what you own, what you owe, and what you might owe

In plain English, a personal balance sheet is a list of everything you own, at what it would sell for today, minus everything you owe. The difference is your net worth. Accountants call the two sides assets and liabilities. That part is simple.

The professional framing adds three disciplines. First, value assets at what they would fetch now, less the cost of selling them, not at what you paid or what you hope. Second, list liabilities at what it would take to clear them today, including any prepayment penalty. Third, add a separate line for contingent liabilities: debts that are not yours today but become yours if something goes wrong. The most important one for a developer is a personal guarantee on a project loan. It does not show up in your net worth until the day it does, and then it can be larger than everything else on the page.

Here is a worked example. All numbers are hypothetical. A developer owns a home worth $600,000 with a $400,000 mortgage. He holds a share of a project he could sell for about $300,000, though it would take a year. He has $40,000 in savings and a car worth $30,000 with a $20,000 loan. Assets total $970,000. Liabilities total $420,000. Net worth is $550,000. Underneath, he has personally guaranteed a $2,000,000 construction loan. On paper he is comfortably in the black. In a bad year, he could owe four times his net worth.

Liquid is not the same as rich

Liquidity is how quickly an asset becomes cash at a fair price. Cash in a bank account is liquid. A share in a half-built project is not; selling it quickly means accepting a deep discount, if anyone will buy it at all. A house is somewhere in between.

The idea that follows is the liquidity floor: an amount of cash or near-cash, held outside your deals, that covers your essential spending for a fixed number of months and that no deal is ever allowed to touch. How many months is a judgment, not a standard. Practitioners commonly talk about six to twenty-four months, and a developer whose income arrives in lumps at project milestones usually needs the long end. Treat any figure you hear as commercial practice and test it against your own cash flows.

Second worked example, again hypothetical. The same developer spends $6,000 a month on things he cannot cut: mortgage, insurance, food, utilities, loan payments. He decides on a twelve-month floor, so the floor is $72,000. His savings are $40,000. He is $32,000 below his own floor, while showing a net worth of more than half a million dollars. Nothing about his net worth tells him that. Only the liquidity view does.

Say that out loud now.

Say it in one breath: "Net worth is what I would have if I sold everything calmly. Liquidity is what I have if I must pay this month."

Concentration: the bet you did not notice you made

Concentration is the share of your wealth that depends on a single asset, sponsor, market or outcome. In the example, $300,000 of a $550,000 net worth sits in one project. That is about 55 percent. Add the guarantee, and the home in the same city, and the developer's fees from the same deal, and almost everything he has is one bet on one market.

The professional way to see this is to ask what moves together. Two assets are effectively one bet if the same event knocks both down. A local recession reduces your project value, slows your sales, stretches your schedule, raises the chance the guarantee is called and lowers the price of your house, all at once. Diversification is not owning many things. It is owning things that do not fail for the same reason.

Concentration is not automatically wrong. Most real wealth is built by concentrating on something you understand. The mistake is concentration you have not chosen, measured and capped. A useful habit is to write down, for each major commitment, the worst realistic outcome and whether you could survive it without breaching your liquidity floor.

How the best do it

Large institutional investors such as insurers and university endowments generally run their portfolios in tiers: cash to meet obligations in the next year or two, liquid investments behind that, and long-dated illiquid assets such as real estate only after the first two are secure. They stress-test what happens if their illiquid holdings cannot be sold for several years. What a small developer can copy is the order of operations: fund the floor first, decide your concentration limit second, and only then decide how much goes into the next deal.

Enough

The last first principle is the hardest. Without a number for enough, every deal looks necessary and every risk looks worth taking. Warrick will not define it for you. Ask yourself: what annual spending would let me live well without anxiety? What would I need to keep doing this work by choice rather than by necessity? What would I refuse to put at risk, at any return? Write your answers down this week. They are the boundaries everything else in this subject is built inside.

A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this; these are concepts, not recommendations.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a cash call arriving when your wealth is all illiquid: a guarantee called, an equity top-up demanded, an income gap during a slow lease-up. Forced sellers sell at the worst price. The control is a written liquidity floor, held in a separate account, sized to your real essential spending, reviewed every quarter and protected by a rule that no deal may draw on it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads net worth and stops. He counts project equity at its hoped-for completion value, leaves the personal guarantee off the page because it "will never be called", and treats a big paper number as permission to commit more. Then the first delay turns a rich man into a desperate one in a single quarter.

Callback

In Week 2 you met the outside view: before trusting your own forecast, ask how projects like this one usually turn out. Apply the same idea here. Your plan says the project equity will be sold at completion. The outside view asks how often projects like it run late, need more equity or sell for less than planned. Your liquidity floor should be sized for that reference class, not for your plan.

Recap

A personal balance sheet has three columns that matter: what you own at today's selling value, what you owe, and what you might owe through guarantees. Net worth shows the size of your wealth; liquidity shows whether it can pay this month's bills; concentration shows how many of your eggs share one basket. Fund the floor first, cap concentration second, invest third, and decide what enough means to you.

Next lesson: Ford, with Roman assisting, takes apart a real failure of concentration and liquidity: Olympia and York, 1992.
checklist: List every asset at today's selling value, less selling costs, not at cost or hoped-for value.
List every liability at today's payoff amount, including penalties.
List every personal guarantee and contingent liability on a separate line with its maximum amount.
Calculate monthly essential spending from real statements, not memory.
Set a written liquidity floor in months and dollars, and hold it in a separate account.
Measure concentration: the share of net worth tied to your largest single bet and market.
Write your own answer to what enough means, and date it.
Book a quarterly review of this sheet, and see a licensed adviser before acting.
head: Field checklist
speak: My personal balance sheet is the first project I manage. Net worth is what I own at today's selling value minus what I owe, but it hides two dangers. The first is liquidity: how fast I can turn assets into cash at a fair price. A share in a half-built project is not cash, and a guarantee on a construction loan can become my debt overnight. So I hold a liquidity floor, months of essential spending in a separate account that no deal may touch. The second danger is concentration: how much of my wealth depends on one project and one market. If my equity, my fees, my house and my guarantee all fall in the same local downturn, I have one bet, not four assets. I fund the floor first, cap concentration second, and invest third. And I write down what enough means to me, because without it every risk looks worth taking.
terms: Personal balance sheet — a statement of everything you own at today's selling value and everything you owe, including what you might owe under guarantees.
Liquidity floor — a set amount of cash or near-cash, held outside your deals, that covers essential spending for a chosen number of months and is never used for a deal.
Concentration — the share of your wealth that depends on a single asset, market or outcome, so that one event could damage most of it at once.

hostile.q: Your personal financial statement shows a net worth of over half a million dollars. Why should I believe you can actually support this guarantee?
hostile.a: You should not rely on the net worth line alone, and I do not. Here is the liquidity view: my liquid assets, my monthly essential spending, and the floor I hold that is separate from this project. Here is my contingent liability schedule with every guarantee I have given. I have tested what happens if this project is a year late and needs more equity, and I can show you that I would still meet my obligations without selling my stake at a distressed price. I'll walk you through those numbers now.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman (risk and the lender's view)
title: Olympia and York: the empire that could not wait
summary: In 1992 Olympia and York, one of the largest private property companies in the world, sought court protection from its creditors. Its wealth was real, but it was concentrated in a few giant projects and funded with money that could be called back far sooner than those buildings could be sold or filled. This lesson takes the collapse through seven forensic steps and ends with Rule 7.
body:
Olympia and York did not fail because its buildings were worthless; it failed because its wealth could not be turned into cash as fast as its lenders wanted their money back. Concentration plus a liquidity mismatch can bring down even the strongest name in the business.

Recall

Q. What makes a one-page memo work?

A. The conclusion and the decision you need sit at the top, followed by the few facts that support them, with the detail moved to attachments. A reader who stops after the first paragraph should still be able to act.

Q. What is the pyramid principle?

A. Start with the single governing idea, support it with a small number of grouped reasons, and support each reason with evidence beneath it. The listener always knows where they are in the argument.

Q. What is a pre-mortem?

A. Before committing, the team imagines the project has failed badly and writes down why. It surfaces risks that optimism and politeness would otherwise keep silent.

Why this matters

Every developer eventually becomes the kind of person lenders trust on reputation. That is when this case matters most. Olympia and York was run by the Reichmann family from Toronto and was, by wide account, one of the most admired development companies of its era. Its collapse shows that reputation, scale and real assets do not protect you from a simple arithmetic problem: you cannot pay a debt due next month with a building you can only sell next decade.

Timeline and key decisions

Step 1, the timeline. Through the 1970s and 1980s, Olympia and York grew from a Toronto business into a developer of major office towers in Canada and the United States, including the World Financial Center in Lower Manhattan. In the late 1980s it began Canary Wharf, an enormous office district in London's Docklands, away from the traditional financial centre. The first buildings arrived into a London office market that had turned weak. The major rail link the location depended on had not yet been built. In the spring of 1992, unable to refinance maturing debt, the company sought protection from creditors in Canada, and the Canary Wharf companies went into administration in Britain.

Step 2, the key decisions. Three stand out. First, the decision to take on Canary Wharf, a project of a scale that would put a very large share of the group's fortune into one location in one market. Second, the decision to finance growth substantially with shorter-term borrowing, including commercial paper, which is debt that must be rolled over every few months. Third, the decision to hold large stakes in other businesses, so that the property company's fortunes and those investments became tied together through borrowing.

Roman's note: none of these decisions is foolish on its own. Big projects create big value. Short-term debt is cheaper. The danger lies in the combination.

Assumptions and incentives

Step 3, the assumptions. The plan rested on assumptions that each looked reasonable in a boom. That financial firms would want to move to Canary Wharf. That the London market would absorb millions of square feet. That the new rail link would arrive in time. That short-term lenders would always roll their loans over for a borrower with this reputation. The last one is the deadly one. It assumes the lender's behaviour in a crisis will match its behaviour in good times. It almost never does.

Step 4, the incentives. Lenders competed to lend to a prestigious borrower and, by many reports, accepted less disclosure than they would have demanded from a smaller firm. A private, family-controlled company had no public shareholders asking about concentration. Success had come from bold, contrarian bets, which rewards repeating them. Everyone's incentives pointed toward more growth and less scrutiny.

Warning signs and the point of no return

Step 5, the warning signs ignored. The signs were visible: falling office rents and rising vacancy in London; a new district competing against an established centre; transport commitments still not secured; and a debt structure needing constant refinancing while property values fell. When lenders began to ask questions, the very fact that they were asking was itself the warning. Confidence-based funding disappears all at once.

Say that out loud now.

"A debt that must be refinanced is a bet that tomorrow's lender will be as friendly as today's."

Step 6, the point of no return. The point of no return came when Canary Wharf required large continuing cash while the rest of the group's assets could not be sold quickly at fair prices, and the short-term lenders stopped rolling. From that moment, no amount of underlying asset value could close the timing gap. Notice that the point of no return arrived well before the filing. By then the choices left were all bad.

Root cause and the rule

Step 7, the root cause. The root cause was a mismatch of time and concentration: long-dated, illiquid, concentrated assets funded with liabilities that could be withdrawn quickly, without a reserve large enough to survive a period when markets would not cooperate. The buildings proved their value over the long run; Canary Wharf became a major financial district. The owners simply could not wait long enough to see it.

Now the applied example for you, hypothetical numbers. A small developer has $500,000 of net worth. He commits $400,000 of it as equity to one project, signs a guarantee, and funds his share partly with a $150,000 personal line of credit that the bank can review every year. The project runs a year late. At the annual review, the bank reduces the line. He now owes $150,000 he must repay, has $100,000 outside the project, and his $400,000 is locked in a building with no buyers. He is solvent on paper and out of cash in practice: Olympia and York at a scale of one person.

The prevention is not to avoid big bets. It is to make sure no single bet, and no lender's change of mood, can take everything. Before any commitment, run the worst realistic case: the project a year late, the line of credit reduced, the market down. If that case breaches your liquidity floor, the commitment is too big.

Rule 7: Never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, be able to take everything; size every commitment so its worst case leaves your liquidity floor untouched.

A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financing decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is funding a long, illiquid bet with money that can be called back sooner than the bet can be sold. The control is to match the term of your funding to the life of the asset where you can, hold a liquidity floor outside the deal, and stress-test every commitment against a delay plus a funding withdrawal at the same time.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads this story and concludes that the Reichmanns were reckless or unlucky. They were neither in any simple sense. The beginner's mistake is believing that a strong reputation or a valuable asset protects you from a liquidity crisis. Lenders who are friendly in good times can all leave in the same month.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied loss aversion and the planning fallacy. The planning fallacy makes us expect projects to finish on time and on budget. Loss aversion makes us hold on to a failing bet rather than accept a smaller loss early. Together they explain how capable people end up past the point of no return: the plan said it would work, and stopping meant admitting a loss. A pre-mortem from Week 2 is the tool that asks the hard question before the money is committed.

Recap

Olympia and York collapsed in 1992 because concentrated, long-term, illiquid assets were funded with debt that could be withdrawn quickly. The warning signs were visible: a weakening market, a project depending on infrastructure not yet built, and constant refinancing. The point of no return came before the filing. Rule 7 says to size every commitment so that its worst case leaves your liquidity floor untouched.

Next lesson: Warrick on the money, putting a price on liquidity and concentration.
checklist: For each commitment, write down when its funding could be withdrawn and when the asset could realistically be sold.
Flag any personal borrowing that can be reduced or recalled at a lender's annual review.
Run a combined stress: the project a year late plus a funding source withdrawn.
Confirm the worst case leaves your liquidity floor intact; if not, shrink the commitment.
Count how much of your net worth depends on one project and one market.
Treat a lender asking new questions as a warning sign, not an inconvenience.
See a licensed adviser before taking on personal debt to fund project equity.
head: Field checklist
speak: In 1992 Olympia and York, run by the Reichmann family from Toronto and one of the most admired developers of its time, sought protection from its creditors. Its buildings were real and, in the long run, valuable. Canary Wharf became a major financial district. But the group had concentrated a huge share of its fortune in one giant project, in a London market that had turned weak, while depending on transport that was not yet built. It funded growth with short-term debt that had to be rolled over constantly. When lenders stopped rolling, no amount of long-term value could pay a debt due now. The root cause was a mismatch: long, illiquid, concentrated assets funded by money that could leave quickly, with no reserve to survive the wait. Rule 7: never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, take everything. Size every commitment so its worst case leaves my liquidity floor untouched.
terms: Liquidity mismatch — funding a long-term, hard-to-sell asset with money that can be demanded back much sooner.
Commercial paper — short-term borrowing, usually repaid or rolled over within months, that depends on lenders continuing to buy new paper.
Point of no return — the moment after which every remaining option is bad, usually well before the visible failure.

hostile.q: Your plan depends on refinancing in two years. What happens if the market for that refinancing is closed when you need it?
hostile.a: Then I would be in exactly the position that broke Olympia and York, so I have planned for it. The refinancing is the expected path, not the only one. I have sized the project so it carries itself at a lower debt amount, I hold a reserve outside the deal that covers carrying costs for a set period, and I have a sale-of-units fallback with a price I have tested. I can show you the case where the refinancing is twelve months late and the market is down, and what we would do on each of the first three days of that scenario.

rule: Rule 7: Never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, be able to take everything; size every commitment so its worst case leaves your liquidity floor untouched.

title: Pricing safety: what a liquidity floor costs and what its absence costs
summary: A liquidity floor is not free: money held safe earns less than money in a deal. But being forced to sell, or being unable to meet a guarantee, costs far more and can end a career. This lesson puts numbers on both sides, shows why averages hide ruin, and closes with Warrick's first Wealth Ledger.
body:
Safety has a price you can see every year and a payoff you only see in a crisis. The developer who prices both sides honestly holds more cash than the spreadsheet seems to want, and stays in the game long enough to compound.

Recall

Q. In a tense meeting, what does "I'll confirm by Friday" do for you?

A. It turns a question you cannot answer accurately into a specific commitment with a date. It protects your credibility far better than guessing, as long as you then deliver by Friday.

Q. When presenting a number aloud, how do you help the listener hold it?

A. Round it, say what it is compared with, and say what it means before moving on. One number per sentence, with a pause after it.

Q. Name two value levers a developer controls.

A. Among others: what you pay for land, what you build and for how much, how fast you lease or sell, and how the project is financed. Each moves the gap between cost and finished value.

Why this matters

Every dollar in your liquidity floor is a dollar not in your next deal, and your spreadsheet will remind you of that every time. If you cannot put a number on what the floor buys you, you will slowly spend it on opportunities. This lesson gives you the arithmetic so the floor survives contact with a good-looking deal.

The visible cost: cash drag

Cash drag is the return you give up by holding money somewhere safe instead of somewhere productive. It is an opportunity cost: nobody sends you a bill, but you are poorer than you would have been.

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer holds a $72,000 floor in an account earning 3 percent a year. If he put the same money into a project he expects to return 15 percent a year, the difference is 12 percentage points. Twelve percent of $72,000 is $8,640 a year. Over three years, ignoring compounding to keep it simple, the floor costs about $26,000 in returns he did not earn.

That number is real, and you should know it. Notice two things about it. First, the 15 percent is an expectation, not a promise; it is the return if the project goes well. Second, the cost is spread evenly across good years and bad. You pay a little every year whether you need the floor or not, exactly like an insurance premium.

The hidden cost: being forced

The forced-sale discount is the gap between what an asset is worth to a patient seller and what it fetches when the seller must have cash now. Buyers can smell urgency. A share in an unfinished project, sold in a hurry during a downturn, may attract a fraction of its fair value or no offer at all.

Worked example, hypothetical. Without a floor, the same developer hits a cash call. His project stake is fairly worth $300,000, but a quick sale draws offers 30 percent below that. He loses $90,000 in one transaction. Suppose, after studying projects like his, he believes there is about a one-in-five chance of facing a cash call he cannot otherwise meet during a three-year hold. The expected loss is one-fifth of $90,000, or $18,000.

On those numbers, the floor costs about $26,000 and saves an expected $18,000. A naive reading says the floor is a bad deal. That reading is wrong, and the reason is the most important idea in this lesson.

Say that out loud now.

"An average only helps me if I survive to collect it."

Why averages hide ruin

Risk of ruin is the chance of a loss so large that you cannot continue: you lose the deal, default on a guarantee, damage your name with lenders, or are forced out of the business. Expected-value arithmetic treats a loss as something you can average away over many tries. Ruin is different. After ruin, there are no more tries.

Look again at the example. The $90,000 discount is the mild version. The severe version is that no buyer appears, the guarantee is called, and the developer must pay the lender from assets he does not have in cash. Now the outcome is not a discount; it is a default, legal costs, and years of lenders treating him as a risk. That tail is hard to put a number on, which is exactly why it gets left out of the spreadsheet.

There is also simple arithmetic that punishes deep losses. If you lose 50 percent of your wealth, you need a 100 percent gain just to get back to where you started. If you lose 80 percent, you need a 400 percent gain. Losses and gains are not symmetrical. Avoiding the deep loss is worth more than an equal-sized gain.

Concentration and the return you actually earn

Your personal return is not the project's internal rate of return (IRR), the annualised return a project produces on the money invested in it. It is the result across everything you own. A brilliant project IRR on 80 percent of your net worth is a very different personal bet from the same IRR on 20 percent.

Worked example, hypothetical. Two developers each have $500,000. Developer A puts $450,000 into one project. Developer B puts $250,000 into the same project and keeps $250,000 outside it, part as a floor and part in assets that do not depend on that market. If the project returns 50 percent over its life, A gains $225,000 and B gains $125,000. A looks smarter. If the project loses half its value, A loses $225,000, nearly half his wealth, and is exposed if more cash is needed. B loses $125,000, a quarter of his wealth, and still holds the cash to protect his position, perhaps even to buy a distressed partner out. In the good case A wins by $100,000. In the bad case B is still in business.

Professionals sum this up as sizing positions so that no single outcome can end the career. The precise limit is a judgment and commercial practice, not a rule anyone can give you. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, the floor appears as a low-yielding asset, and that is correct. Do not try to make it look productive. What belongs next to it is a note that records what it protects: the guarantees it stands behind, the months of spending it covers, and the date you last tested it. Your project equity belongs on the sheet at a cautious value with its expected sale date and its forced-sale value both written down. The gap between those two numbers is your exposure to timing. When that gap is large and your floor is thin, your real wealth is smaller than your net worth line says.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting the visible cost of the floor win every argument, so it is spent bit by bit on attractive deals until a cash call finds it gone. The control is a written policy: the floor's size, what it is for, the only events that may draw on it, and the rule that it is rebuilt before any new commitment is made.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares the floor's cost to its expected benefit, finds the floor expensive, and cuts it. He has averaged away the one outcome that cannot be averaged: being forced out of the game. Ask not "what does the floor earn?" but "what does its absence put at risk?"

Callback

Four lessons ago, in Week 6, you practised presenting numbers aloud. Use that skill here. When a partner says the floor is "dead money", say: "It costs us about nine thousand dollars a year. It protects a three-hundred-thousand-dollar stake from a fire sale and a two-million-dollar guarantee from being called on us with no cash. That is the cheapest insurance in the business." One number, one comparison, one meaning.

Recap

The liquidity floor has a visible cost, cash drag, that you pay every year. Its absence carries a hidden cost, the forced-sale discount, and a far larger one, the risk of ruin, that expected-value arithmetic hides. Losses and gains are not symmetrical, and your personal return depends on how much of your wealth one project carries.

Next lesson: Omar on the rules, the legal shape of a personal balance sheet, including what a personal guarantee really commits you to.
checklist: Calculate the annual cash drag of your liquidity floor in dollars.
Estimate the forced-sale value of each illiquid asset, not just its fair value.
Write down the severe case for each guarantee: no buyer, guarantee called, no cash.
Check what loss would require a doubling just to recover, and whether any single deal could cause it.
Size each project commitment as a share of total net worth, not as a share of the deal.
Write a floor policy: size, purpose, permitted draws, and rebuild-before-new-deal rule.
Review the policy with a licensed adviser before acting on it.
head: Field checklist
speak: A liquidity floor costs money every year. If I hold seventy-two thousand dollars earning three percent instead of putting it in a deal I expect to return fifteen, I give up about nine thousand dollars a year. That is cash drag, and it is real. But being forced to sell an unfinished project stake in a downturn can cost thirty percent of its value in one go, and the severe case is worse: no buyer, the guarantee called, and no cash to pay it. Expected-value arithmetic can make the floor look like a bad deal, because it averages that outcome away. An average only helps me if I survive to collect it. Losses and gains are not symmetrical: lose half and I need to double just to get back. So I size every position so no single outcome can end my career, and I treat the floor as the cheapest insurance in the business.
terms: Cash drag — the return given up by holding money in a safe, low-yielding place instead of a productive investment.
Forced-sale discount — the gap between an asset's fair value to a patient seller and the price it fetches when the seller must raise cash quickly.
Risk of ruin — the chance of a loss so large that you cannot continue, which cannot be averaged away because there are no further attempts after it.

hostile.q: You're keeping a large cash reserve outside the deal. Isn't that just lazy capital dragging down your returns?
hostile.a: It costs us a known amount every year, and I can tell you the figure. What it buys is the ability to meet a cash call without selling our stake at a fire-sale price or defaulting on a guarantee. The expected saving alone does not cover the cost, but the expected saving is not the point. The point is that the reserve removes the outcome that ends a developer's career. I would rather earn a slightly lower return for many years than a higher one for a few.

title: Who owns what: guarantees, title and the legal shape of your wealth
summary: Your balance sheet has a legal shape as well as a numerical one: how each asset is held, who can claim it, and what you have promised to pay if someone else does not. This lesson explains personal guarantees, joint and several liability, and the duty of honesty in a personal financial statement, as concepts to discuss with a lawyer.
body:
Two balance sheets with the same numbers can carry very different risks, because what matters in a crisis is who legally owns each asset and who can legally come after it. Read the legal shape of your wealth as carefully as the totals.

Recall

Q. What is a sound structure for explaining a subject in two minutes?

A. One-sentence bottom line, three supporting points, one concrete example, and a close that states the decision or the ask.

Q. What is the rule of three in communication?

A. Listeners hold three points far more easily than five, so group your reasons into three. If you have more, merge them.

Q. What does the incentives lens ask in a deal?

A. Who gets paid, when, and for what. People tend to do what they are paid to do, so read the incentives before you read the promises.

Why this matters

Most developers sign their first personal guarantee within a few years of starting out. It is often treated as a formality the bank requires. It is not a formality. It is a promise that can reach your house, your savings and your future income. Understanding the legal shape of your wealth is how you know, before you sign, what you are actually putting on the table.

A note on scope. Omar teaches concepts here. The law differs between jurisdictions and changes over time. Verify any point against the primary source before you rely on it, and get advice on your specific documents. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in the relevant jurisdiction.

The personal guarantee

In plain English, a personal guarantee is your promise to pay someone else's debt if they do not. In development, that someone is usually your own project company. You form a company to borrow and build, partly so that the company's debts stay inside the company. The lender then asks you to guarantee those debts personally, which reaches straight back through that protection to you.

The professional framing has four questions to put to any guarantee, each answered by its wording. How much: is it limited to a fixed amount or a percentage, or is it for the whole debt, interest and costs? What triggers it: any default, or only specific events such as fraud or failing to complete? When it ends: at completion, at a debt ratio being reached, or never? And what the lender must do first: must it pursue the company and the property before coming to you, or can it come to you directly? In many documents the answer to the last question is that the lender may come to you first. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer guarantees a $2,000,000 construction loan. Version one is unlimited and lasts until the loan is repaid. Version two is capped at 25 percent of the loan, or $500,000, and falls away once the building is complete and leased to an agreed level. On a balance sheet both appear as "personal guarantee". Legally, the first can reach everything he owns for years; the second has a ceiling and an end date. The percentage, the trigger and the burn-off are commercial terms negotiated with the lender, not standards.

Joint and several liability

When two or more people guarantee the same debt, the wording usually makes them liable jointly and severally. In plain English, that means the lender can collect the whole amount from all of them together, or from any one of them alone. You may think of yourself as responsible for your half. The lender may be entitled to see you as responsible for all of it.

Worked example, hypothetical. Two partners jointly and severally guarantee $1,000,000. One partner has spent his money and has little left. The lender, if the wording allows, can pursue the partner who still has assets for the full $1,000,000. That partner may then have a claim against the other for his share, but a claim against someone with nothing is worth very little. The practical lesson: when you co-guarantee, you are guaranteeing your partner's balance sheet as well as the project.

Say that out loud now.

"Jointly and severally means the lender can take it all from me."

How assets are held, and the honest statement

The legal form of ownership matters. An asset in your sole name is generally reachable by your personal creditors. An asset held jointly with another person may carry rights for that person. An asset held by a company is owned by the company, not by you; what you own is the shares. Each form has different consequences for creditors, for tax, and for what happens when you die, which is next week's subject. Choosing a form after a problem appears is a different matter from choosing it before. Transfers made to keep assets away from a creditor you already owe can be undone in many legal systems. That is why structure is designed early, a subject that returns in depth much later in the course.

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer owns two rental condominiums of similar value. He holds the first in his own name. He holds the second through a small company of which he owns all the shares, and the company's only debt is its own mortgage, which he has not guaranteed. A tenant is injured and sues. A claim arising from the first unit is a claim against him personally, and if it exceeds his insurance it can reach his other personal assets. A claim arising from the second unit is, in principle, a claim against the company, and his exposure is generally limited to the value of his shares, unless he has signed something that reaches back to him or the company has been run in a way a court will not respect. The second outcome depends on keeping the company genuinely separate: its own bank account, its own records, its own contracts. Verify how this works in your jurisdiction against the primary source before you rely on it.

The second rule concerns honesty. Lenders often ask for a personal financial statement, your own signed summary of your assets and liabilities. It is a representation: a statement of fact that the lender relies on. Overstating values, leaving out a guarantee, or forgetting a debt can expose you to serious consequences, and a lender who discovers it will rarely trust you again. The control is simple. Use the same cautious values you use privately, list every contingent liability, date the statement, and keep the working papers.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a guarantee whose cap, trigger and end date you never read, alongside partners whose balance sheets you never checked. The control is a guarantee schedule: every guarantee you have given, its maximum amount, its triggers, its end conditions, who else is on it, and the date your lawyer reviewed it, updated before you sign anything new.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks forming a company means his personal assets are protected, then signs a full personal guarantee that removes that protection for the largest debt the company has. The company protects you only from the debts you have not personally guaranteed.

Callback

In Week 1 you met every seat at the development table. The lender's seat looks at a deal and asks: if this goes wrong, who pays us back, and how? The personal guarantee is the lender's answer to that question. When you understand why the lender wants it, you can negotiate it: a cap, a narrower trigger, a burn-off at completion. Treating it as a fixed requirement leaves those levers untouched.

Recap

A personal guarantee is a promise to pay a debt if your company does not; its real size depends on its cap, its triggers, its end date, and whether the lender must pursue others first. Joint and several liability means any one guarantor can be made to pay all of it. How assets are held decides who can reach them, and a personal financial statement is a representation you must make honestly. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in the relevant jurisdiction.

Next lesson: Nadia on the numbers, building a personal balance sheet and liquidity floor step by step.
checklist: Keep a guarantee schedule: amount, cap, triggers, end conditions, co-guarantors and review date.
Read whether the lender must pursue the company and property before coming to you.
Check whether any co-guarantee is joint and several, and check each co-guarantor's balance sheet.
Record how each asset is legally held: sole name, joint, or through a company.
Never move assets around after a problem appears; design structure before it is needed.
Prepare every personal financial statement with cautious values and every contingent liability listed.
Have a licensed lawyer review each guarantee before you sign it.
head: Field checklist
speak: A personal guarantee is my promise to pay a debt if my project company does not. It reaches straight back through the protection the company gives me. Its real size depends on four things in the wording: the cap, what triggers it, when it ends, and whether the lender can come to me first. An unlimited guarantee lasting until repayment and a capped guarantee that burns off at completion both say personal guarantee on a balance sheet, but they are very different promises, and those terms are negotiable commercial practice. When partners guarantee together, joint and several liability usually means the lender can take the whole amount from any one of us, so I am guaranteeing my partner's balance sheet too. How I hold assets decides who can reach them, and a personal financial statement is a representation I must make honestly. A licensed lawyer reviews every guarantee before I sign.
terms: Personal guarantee — a personal promise to pay a debt if the borrower, often your own company, fails to pay.
Joint and several liability — a liability that the creditor can collect in full from all the obligors together or from any one of them alone.
Representation — a statement of fact in a document that the other party is entitled to rely on, such as the values in a personal financial statement.

hostile.q: We need a full, unlimited personal guarantee from you. Every developer gives one. Why are you pushing back?
hostile.a: I understand why you want recourse to me, and I am willing to give a guarantee. What I am asking is that it match the risk you are worried about. Your biggest risk is that the building is not completed; once it is complete and leased, the property itself carries the loan. So I propose a guarantee capped at an agreed amount, covering completion and cost overruns, that falls away when the building reaches an agreed occupancy. I'll have my lawyer send proposed wording by Friday.

title: Building the sheet: net worth, liquid net worth and the concentration ratio
summary: A step-by-step worked calculation of a hypothetical developer's personal balance sheet: selling costs, liquidity haircuts, liquid net worth, the liquidity floor and the concentration ratio. Then a stress test shows how a comfortable-looking sheet breaks when one guarantee is called.
body:
The same balance sheet gives three different answers depending on the question you ask: how much am I worth, how much could I pay this month, and how much rides on one bet. Calculate all three, every time, in that order.

Recall

Q. What is a liquidity floor?

A. A set amount of cash or near-cash, held outside your deals, covering essential spending for a chosen number of months, which no deal is ever allowed to touch.

Q. When you speak a calculation aloud, why pause after each number?

A. Because the listener needs a moment to hold it before the next one arrives. A pause turns a stream of digits into a sequence of facts.

Q. What does an after-action review ask?

A. What did we expect, what actually happened, why was there a difference, and what will we do differently next time. It is run without blame so people tell the truth.

Why this matters

A developer who cannot produce his own balance sheet in an hour cannot answer a lender's first question with confidence, and cannot tell whether the next deal is affordable. The calculation below takes about thirty minutes once you have your statements in front of you. Do it once properly and updating it each quarter takes ten minutes.

Every number that follows is hypothetical and rounded. The percentages for selling costs and haircuts are illustrations, not standards; use quotes or evidence for your own assets.

Steps 1 to 4: from fair value to net worth

Step 1. List every asset at fair value today. Home $600,000. Share of a development project $300,000. Bank savings $40,000. An investment account $60,000. Car $30,000.

Step 2. Deduct the cost of selling. A home sale carries agent and legal costs; assume 6 percent, or $36,000, leaving $564,000. The project share, sold to a partner under the partnership agreement, assume 3 percent, $9,000, leaving $291,000. Cash costs nothing to sell. The investment account, assume nothing. The car, assume 10 percent lost to a quick sale, leaving $27,000. Total assets, net of selling costs: $564,000 plus $291,000 plus $40,000 plus $60,000 plus $27,000 equals $982,000.

Step 3. List liabilities at today's payoff. Mortgage $400,000. Car loan $20,000. Credit card $5,000. Total $425,000.

Step 4. Net worth equals assets minus liabilities. $982,000 minus $425,000 equals $557,000. That is the headline number, the one people quote.

Steps 5 to 8: liquidity and the floor

Step 5. Apply a haircut to anything you might need to sell fast. A haircut is a deliberate reduction in an asset's value to reflect what it might fetch when you need cash in a bad market. Cash takes no haircut: $40,000. The investment account could fall in exactly the downturn that creates your cash need, so take a 20 percent haircut: $48,000. The home and project share are excluded entirely, because they cannot become cash within thirty days at anything near fair value. Liquid assets: $40,000 plus $48,000 equals $88,000.

Step 6. Subtract debts due within the year that liquid assets would have to cover. The credit card, $5,000. Liquid net worth is $88,000 minus $5,000, or $83,000.

Step 7. Calculate essential monthly spending. Mortgage $2,500, car loan $500, insurance $400, food, utilities and other necessities $2,600. Total $6,000 a month.

Step 8. Set the floor and compare. At a twelve-month floor chosen for lumpy developer income, the floor is 12 times $6,000, or $72,000. Liquid net worth of $83,000 covers it with $11,000 to spare. On this view, he is fine, narrowly.

Say that out loud now.

"Net worth five hundred and fifty-seven thousand. Liquid net worth eighty-three thousand. Floor seventy-two thousand. Spare eleven thousand."

Steps 9 and 10: concentration and the stress test

Step 9. Calculate the concentration ratio. The concentration ratio is your exposure to a single bet divided by your net worth. Start with the equity: $291,000 divided by $557,000 is about 52 percent. Now add what he has promised on the same project. He has personally guaranteed 25 percent of a $2,000,000 construction loan, a cap of $500,000. Total exposure to the one project is $291,000 plus $500,000, or $791,000. Divided by net worth of $557,000, that is about 142 percent. More than all of his net worth depends on one building.

Step 10. Run a stress case. The project runs late and over budget. The lender calls on the guarantee for a $150,000 cost overrun. The project share cannot be sold for months, and then only at a deep discount. He must pay from liquid net worth: $83,000 minus $150,000 leaves him $67,000 short. His floor is gone, he owes more than he has in cash, and he still has his $6,000 of monthly bills.

Here is the second worked example: the same sheet, adjusted before signing. Suppose he negotiates the guarantee cap down to $250,000 and the lender agrees it falls away once the building is complete. He also holds back $100,000 of his planned equity and keeps it as cash, contributing $200,000 instead of $300,000, with a partner taking the balance. Now liquid net worth is roughly $183,000, and concentration including the guarantee is about $194,000 of equity plus $250,000 of guarantee, $444,000, divided by roughly $557,000, which is about 80 percent. The same $150,000 overrun now leaves $33,000 in cash: below his floor, but survivable, with the share still his to sell calmly. He gave up some upside and kept his career.

Reading the three answers

Professionally, you read the three numbers in a fixed order and write one sentence about each. Net worth: how large is my wealth on a calm day? Liquid net worth against the floor: can I pay my obligations without selling anything at a loss? Concentration with contingent exposure: what is the largest single event that could hurt me, and how big is it compared with everything I own? A sheet is only healthy if all three sentences are acceptable.

Keep the working papers behind every figure: the statement or quote that supports each value, the reason for each haircut, and the date. Each quarter, update the values first, then the three sentences, and compare them with last quarter's. The trend matters as much as the level. A liquid net worth falling for three quarters in a row is a warning even while it is still above the floor. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of these figures.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving contingent liabilities off the concentration ratio, which makes a dangerous position look moderate. The control is a fixed template: every guarantee is added at its cap to the exposure for the project it supports, and the stress test always includes at least one guarantee being called while the related equity cannot be sold.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts the house and the project share as if they were cash, because they appear as large numbers on the sheet. Ask of every asset: could I turn this into cash in thirty days, in a bad month, at close to the value written here? If not, it does not belong in liquid net worth.

Callback

In Week 5 you learned to put the bottom line first. Apply it to your own sheet. Do not open with the list of assets. Open with the conclusion: "My net worth is about five hundred and sixty thousand, my liquid position covers my floor with a little to spare, and my biggest exposure is one project at roughly eighty percent of net worth including the guarantee." Then give the detail to anyone who asks.

Recap

Value assets at fair value less selling costs, list liabilities at payoff, and subtract to get net worth. Apply haircuts and exclude illiquid assets to get liquid net worth, and compare it with a floor based on real monthly spending. Add each guarantee at its cap to calculate the concentration ratio, then stress-test with a guarantee called while the equity cannot be sold. Change the commitment before signing if the stress case breaks you.

Next lesson: Roman in the room, sitting across from a lender who wants your personal financial statement and your guarantee.
checklist: Gather current statements for every account, loan and asset before you start.
Deduct a realistic selling cost from every asset you would have to sell.
Apply a haircut to anything whose price could fall when you most need cash.
Exclude anything that cannot become cash within thirty days at near fair value from liquid net worth.
Base the floor on real essential spending multiplied by your chosen number of months.
Add every guarantee at its cap to the exposure for its project when calculating concentration.
Stress-test with one guarantee called while the related equity cannot be sold.
Write one sentence each on net worth, liquidity and concentration, and review with a licensed adviser.
head: Field checklist
speak: I build my balance sheet in ten steps. List assets at fair value, deduct selling costs, list liabilities at payoff, and subtract: in my hypothetical, net worth is about five hundred and fifty-seven thousand. Then I ask what I could pay this month. Cash counts in full, an investment account gets a twenty percent haircut, and the house and project share are excluded. Liquid net worth is eighty-three thousand against a floor of seventy-two thousand, twelve months of six thousand in essential spending. Then concentration: the project equity is about half my net worth, but add the guarantee at its cap and my exposure to one building is a hundred and forty percent of everything I own. Stress it with a hundred-and-fifty-thousand-dollar guarantee call and I am sixty-seven thousand short. Cut the guarantee cap and hold back some equity, and the same shock is survivable.
terms: Haircut — a deliberate reduction in an asset's value to reflect what it might fetch if sold quickly in a bad market.
Liquid net worth — assets that can become cash quickly at near fair value, after haircuts, minus debts due soon that they would have to cover.
Concentration ratio — your total exposure to one bet, including guarantees at their caps, divided by your net worth.

hostile.q: You say your net worth is over half a million, but your liquid assets are under a hundred thousand. Which number should I use?
hostile.a: Both, for different questions, and I will tell you which answers yours. Net worth tells you the size of my wealth on a calm day. Liquid net worth tells you what I could pay within a month without selling at a loss, and that is the number that supports a guarantee in a crisis. I have also calculated my exposure to this project including the guarantee cap, and stress-tested a cost-overrun call. Here is the result, and here is the guarantee cap I need for that stress case to leave me solvent.

title: The guarantee meeting: when the lender asks what you are worth
summary: A realistic scene: a credit officer asks for your personal financial statement and a full guarantee. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the lender's question, when to stay silent, and how to stay steady. It closes with this month's thread on family, legacy and what enough means.
body:
When a lender asks what you are worth, the real question is whether you can and will stand behind this loan on its worst day. Answer that question, with evidence, and you control the meeting.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause of the Olympia and York collapse in 1992?

A. Concentrated, long-term, illiquid assets funded with debt that could be withdrawn quickly, with no reserve large enough to survive a period when markets would not cooperate.

Q. What is the difference between listening to reply and listening to understand?

A. Listening to reply means preparing your answer while the other person talks. Listening to understand means hearing their concern fully, then checking you have it right before you respond.

Q. What does stress reappraisal mean?

A. Treating the racing heart and alertness before a hard moment as your body preparing to perform, rather than as a sign that something is wrong. It is a technique supported by research, not a cure-all.

Why this matters

The guarantee conversation sets the terms of your personal risk for the life of a loan. Developers who treat it as paperwork sign whatever is put in front of them. Developers who prepare for it can usually narrow the guarantee, protect their liquidity floor and leave the lender more confident, not less. The difference is preparation and composure, both learnable.

The scene

This is a composite scene. You sit in a small meeting room with a credit officer from a regional bank and her colleague who handles construction loans. The term sheet is on the table. The project is a hypothetical twenty-unit apartment building. The loan is $4,000,000. The credit officer says: "Before we take this to credit committee, we need your personal financial statement and a full, unconditional guarantee. Standard for a borrower of your size."

Notice what is happening. "Standard" is an anchor, an opening position presented as a fact. "Full and unconditional" is the bank's best case, not its only acceptable case. And "a borrower of your size" is a polite way of saying the bank does not yet know you well enough to rely on the project alone.

The question behind the question

Roman, who has sat on the lender's side, puts it this way. The officer has to defend this loan to a credit committee that will ask three things. If the project fails, how do we get repaid? Is the sponsor honest about his finances? And will the sponsor walk away, or stay and fix the problem? The guarantee answers the first question badly and expensively. It is a blunt tool the bank reaches for when it lacks better comfort on the second and third.

So your job is to answer all three questions so well that a narrower guarantee is enough.

Lines to say.

  • "I understand you need recourse to me. Let me show you what I can support, so you can defend it at committee."
  • "Here is my personal financial statement, with a guarantee schedule listing every guarantee I have already given."
  • "This page shows my liquid position separately from my net worth, and the reserve I hold outside this project."
  • "Your largest risk is completion. I will guarantee completion and cost overruns up to an agreed cap. Once the building reaches an agreed occupancy, the property carries the loan."
  • "If something goes wrong, here is what I will do in the first thirty days."

Lines never to say.

  • "Fine, whatever you need." You have just signed away your floor.
  • "That guarantee will never be called." The officer has seen many that were.
  • "My net worth is over half a million," without the liquidity view. It invites the question you have not prepared for.
  • "Other banks don't ask for this." Unless you can prove it with a term sheet, it sounds like a bluff.
  • Any number you have not checked. A wrong figure on a personal financial statement is a misrepresentation, not a slip.

Say that out loud now.

Say the completion line aloud three times until it sounds calm, not rehearsed: "Your largest risk is completion. I will guarantee completion and cost overruns up to an agreed cap."

Silence and state

When you propose the capped guarantee, stop talking. The officer will need a moment to consider it, and the instinct to fill the silence with a concession is strong. Count to five in your head. The first person to fill the gap usually gives something away.

Stay silent, too, when you are asked a question you cannot answer precisely. Pause, then say: "I want to give you the exact figure. I'll confirm by Friday." That is not weakness; it is the habit of a borrower whose statements can be relied on.

As for your state: the bank will notice composure more than any single answer. Before the meeting, sit in your parked car for two minutes and breathe slowly, with a longer out-breath than in-breath. Never do this while driving. If your heart is racing as you walk in, tell yourself it is your body preparing to perform. Check with your doctor about any breathing practice if you have a medical condition.

A worked second example, hypothetical. Suppose the officer replies: "Committee will want at least 50 percent." You have a choice. You can accept, if your stress test shows a $2,000,000 cap still leaves your floor intact. Or you can trade: "I can go to 35 percent if the guarantee falls away at 90 percent occupancy rather than at loan repayment." Either answer is strong because it comes from numbers you calculated before you walked in. The percentages here are commercial terms, not standards.

Thread: family, legacy and what enough means

Once a month the course steps back from the deal to the person doing it. This month's question sits underneath the guarantee meeting. Every guarantee is a decision about how much of your life's work you are willing to place behind one building. That decision cannot be made well without knowing what the work is for.

So the question is yours to answer, not the course's: what would enough look like for you, and for the people you care about? What would you want to be true in twenty years that no deal could put at risk? Write a few honest sentences. Revisit them before you sign your next guarantee.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is walking into this meeting without your own numbers, so the bank's opening position becomes the deal. The control is to arrive with a finished personal financial statement, a guarantee schedule, a liquidity view and a stress test that tells you the largest guarantee you can afford, and a proposed cap and burn-off ready in writing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the guarantee as the bank's decision and argues emotionally about fairness. The professional treats it as a negotiation about which risk the guarantee covers, and offers the lender better comfort on honesty and commitment in exchange for a narrower promise.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied anchoring: the first number or position stated pulls every later discussion toward it. "Standard full guarantee" is an anchor. You do not beat an anchor by ignoring it. You acknowledge it and replace it with your own evidence-based position, so the discussion moves to your number. That is the same acknowledge, bridge, answer pattern from Week 6, used to negotiate rather than defend.

Recap

Behind a request for your personal financial statement and a full guarantee are three committee questions: how do we get repaid, is the sponsor honest, and will the sponsor stay? Answer all three with evidence, propose a guarantee matched to completion risk with a cap and an end date, stay silent after you make the proposal, and never state a number you have not checked.

Next lesson: Kema with six questions, a Red Pen drill on a flawed personal financial summary, and the boardroom drill for the week.
checklist: Arrive with a completed personal financial statement and a guarantee schedule.
Bring the liquidity view separately from net worth, and your reserve outside the project.
Know, from your stress test, the largest guarantee you can afford before you walk in.
Prepare a written proposal: cap, covered risks, and burn-off condition.
Identify the lender's anchor and answer it with your own evidence.
After making your proposal, stop talking and let the silence work.
Say I'll confirm by Friday rather than state any unchecked number.
Prepare your state with slow breathing in the parked car, never while driving.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a lender asks for my personal financial statement and a full guarantee, the real question is whether I can and will stand behind this loan on its worst day. The credit officer has to answer three committee questions: how do we get repaid, is the sponsor honest, and will the sponsor stay and fix problems? A full guarantee is the blunt answer to the first. So I answer all three with evidence: a personal financial statement with every existing guarantee listed, a liquidity view separate from net worth, and a plan for the first thirty days if things go wrong. Then I propose a guarantee matched to the real risk, completion and cost overruns up to a cap, falling away at an agreed occupancy. I never say it will never be called, and I never state a number I have not checked. After I make the proposal, I stop talking.
terms: Credit committee — the group inside a lender that approves loans, to whom the loan officer must justify every risk.
Burn-off — a condition under which a guarantee reduces or falls away, such as completion or reaching an agreed occupancy.
Anchor — an opening number or position, often presented as standard, that pulls the rest of a negotiation toward it.

hostile.q: If you really believe in this project, why won't you give a full guarantee?
hostile.a: I believe in it enough to put my equity in first and to guarantee completion and cost overruns, which is where your real risk lies. What I will not do is promise my entire balance sheet against a building that, once complete and leased, carries the loan on its own merits. A sponsor who over-guarantees can be wiped out by one bad project, and a wiped-out sponsor cannot help you fix anything. A capped guarantee keeps me solvent and committed, which is what you actually need.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 7 review: wealth mindset under pressure
summary: Six questions with answers covering the personal balance sheet, the liquidity floor, concentration, guarantees and the Olympia and York case. A Red Pen drill on a flawed personal financial summary, then a two-minute boardroom drill with a model answer.
body:
This week you learned to manage your own wealth like a project: measure it three ways, protect a floor, cap concentration, read your guarantees and decide what enough means. Today you test whether it has stuck.

Recall

Q. Why can an expected-value calculation make a liquidity floor look like a bad deal?

A. Because it averages the cost of being forced out of the game across many imaginary attempts. After ruin there are no further attempts, so the average hides the outcome that matters most.

Q. What is the purpose of a one-sentence close in a spoken update?

A. To leave the listener with the decision or the ask, so the update ends in action rather than drifting into detail.

Q. What does loss aversion do to a developer holding a failing project?

A. It makes stopping feel worse than continuing, because stopping turns a paper loss into a real one, so people keep funding a failing bet longer than the evidence supports.

Why this matters

Wealth ideas are easy to agree with and hard to apply when a good deal is on the table. Retrieval practice, answering from memory before checking, is one of the better-supported ways to make learning last. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Why is net worth alone a misleading measure of a developer's financial health?

Answer: It values everything as if it could be sold calmly, so it hides liquidity and leaves contingent liabilities such as personal guarantees off the page. A developer can show a large net worth and still be unable to pay a cash call this month.

Question 2. What makes two different assets effectively one bet?

Answer: When the same event damages both. Project equity, development fees, a guarantee and a home in the same local market can all fall in one downturn. Diversification means owning things that do not fail for the same reason.

Question 3. What is Rule 7, and which case produced it?

Answer: Never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, be able to take everything; size every commitment so its worst case leaves your liquidity floor untouched. It came from Olympia and York, which sought creditor protection in 1992 after funding concentrated, long-term assets with short-term debt.

Question 4. What four questions should you put to any personal guarantee?

Answer: How much is it capped at, what triggers it, when does it end, and must the lender pursue the company and the property before coming to you? The wording answers each one, and each is a negotiable commercial term.

Question 5. How do you calculate the concentration ratio properly?

Answer: Add your equity in one project to every guarantee you have given on it, at its cap, then divide by your net worth. Leaving out the guarantee makes the exposure look far smaller than it is.

Question 6. What three questions sit behind a lender's request for a full guarantee?

Answer: How will we get repaid if the project fails? Is the sponsor honest about his finances? Will the sponsor stay and fix problems? Answer all three with evidence and a narrower guarantee often becomes acceptable.

Say that out loud now.

Say Rule 7 from memory, without looking, then check it word for word.

Red Pen drill

Here is a short hypothetical personal financial summary prepared by a developer before a bank meeting. Find the defects before reading the answers.

"Net worth: $1,200,000. This includes my project share at its expected completion value of $700,000. Liquid funds: $150,000, being my savings of $90,000 plus the $60,000 project contingency held in the project account, which I control. My liquidity floor is therefore fully funded. Contingent liabilities: none material. Concentration: my share is only 15 percent of the total development, so the risk is well spread. I have decided that enough, for me, is whatever my adviser says it is."

The defects, revealed.

  1. The project share is valued at completion value, not today's selling value less selling costs, which inflates net worth.
  2. The project contingency is counted as personal liquid funds. It belongs to the project and is committed to it; counting it twice hides a thin floor.
  3. "Fully funded" is asserted without stating monthly essential spending or the number of months, so it cannot be checked.
  4. "Contingent liabilities: none material" almost certainly omits a personal guarantee on the construction loan. On a document a lender relies on, that is a representation problem, not a rounding issue.
  5. Concentration is measured as a share of the development rather than as a share of his own net worth, which is the number that matters. Here roughly $700,000 of $1,200,000, more than half, plus the guarantee.
  6. Enough is handed to an adviser. Advisers help you reach your goals; only you can set them.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes. Try it aloud now, timed, before reading the model.

Model answer: "My bottom line: a developer's personal balance sheet needs to be run like a project, because our biggest risks spread from the deal into our own lives. I measure it three ways. Net worth tells me the size of my wealth on a calm day. Liquid net worth, against a written floor of essential spending, tells me whether I can meet a cash call without selling anything at a loss. The concentration ratio, including every guarantee at its cap, tells me how much rides on one building. Olympia and York in 1992 showed that even the strongest name can fail when concentrated, long-term assets are funded with money that can leave quickly. So my rule is that no single project or lender can take everything: each commitment is sized so its worst case leaves my floor intact. In practice that means negotiating guarantees with a cap and an end date, and sometimes taking a smaller share of a good deal. The ask today is to approve that sizing policy for our next project."

Scoring yourself

Score your boardroom attempt on four points, one to five each. Accuracy: did every fact match the week, including the year of the case and the exact wording of the rule? Structure: did you open with the bottom line, give three supporting points and close with an ask? Numbers: did you name the three measures without drowning the listener in figures? Composure: did you pause after each key point instead of rushing? Any score below four on accuracy means you reread the relevant lesson before trying again. Any score below four on composure means you try again tomorrow, slower. Two attempts a few days apart will teach you more than five attempts in one sitting, because spacing practice out over time is one of the more reliable findings about how memory works.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is knowing these ideas and still overriding them when an attractive deal arrives. The control is to write your floor, your concentration limit and your guarantee limit down now, while no deal is in front of you, and to require that any exception be written and dated before you sign.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the answers before attempting the questions and mistakes recognition for recall. Cover the answers, say yours aloud, then check.

Callback

In Week 2 you started a decision journal. Use it now. Record your floor, your concentration limit and your answer to what enough means, with today's date and your reasons. In a year, when a deal tempts you past those limits, the journal will show you what you believed when you were calm.

Recap

Measure your wealth three ways: net worth, liquid net worth against a floor, and concentration including guarantees. Price safety honestly; averages hide ruin. Read every guarantee for cap, trigger, end and order of recourse. In the room, answer the lender's real questions with evidence and propose a guarantee matched to the real risk. Decide for yourself what enough means.

head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned to run my own balance sheet like a project. Net worth shows the size of my wealth on a calm day, but it hides liquidity and leaves guarantees off the page. So I also measure liquid net worth against a written floor of essential spending, and a concentration ratio that adds every guarantee at its cap to my equity in a project. Olympia and York in 1992 showed that concentrated, long-term assets funded with money that can leave quickly can bring down even the strongest name. Rule 7: never let one project or one lender's change of mind take everything. In practice I negotiate guarantees with a cap and an end date, answer a lender's real questions with evidence, and sometimes take a smaller share of a good deal. And I decide for myself what enough means.
terms: Retrieval practice — answering from memory before checking, a well-supported way to strengthen learning.
Exception register — a written, dated record of any decision to go beyond a limit you set in advance, with the reason.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes yours only if something else happens, such as a guarantee being called.

hostile.q: You've set yourself a concentration limit. What will you do when the best deal of your career needs more than that limit?
hostile.a: I will treat the limit as the default and any breach as a deliberate, written exception, decided before I sign and not in the excitement of the deal. The first question will be whether I can bring in a partner, reduce my share or narrow the guarantee so the deal fits. If it still does not fit, I will record why I believe the exception is justified and what I will do if it goes wrong, and I will review it with a licensed adviser. Most of the time, the right answer is a smaller share of a great deal.
